messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Dr. Tran is a 77-year-old retired surgeon who spent decades in the operating rooms of a major metropolitan hospital. The event that haunts him occurred twenty years ago, when a faulty piece of equipment sparked a fire in the surgical wing during a late-night procedure. He was not the primary surgeon at the table, but he was first into the adjacent room after the alarm. He saw colleagues dragging patients from the smoke, and he remembers the distinct, acrid smell of burnt flesh and the wave of heat that pressed against his skin. Several patients did not survive. That night, he told himself he had to keep working, to stay calm—and for years, he did.

In the months that followed, he began noticing odd reactions. The olfactory cue of burnt cautery smoke in the OR would strike him without warning, and his body would lurch into a startle response before his mind could place why. Over time, the stress of routine surgeries itself became a trigger, and he found his hands trembling slightly when he scrubbed in. He told himself to push those reactions aside. He tried hard not to think about the fire, and whenever a positive feeling arose—pride in a successful procedure, joy at a patient’s recovery—he pushed it away because it felt unsafe, as though allowing himself to feel good might invite another disaster. He also stopped watching television programmes or films that depicted hospital emergencies or any kind of fire.

But the avoidance only narrowed his world. A certain temperature of steam from an autoclave could send him into full alert, and he began to interpret his own body’s reactions as evidence that something was fundamentally wrong with him. He came to believe that he was defective—that a real surgeon would have handled the trauma without falling apart. This conviction that he was defective seemed to sharpen the memory, making it surface more often and with greater emotional force, as if his failure itself was the event he kept reliving. Because he could not trust his body, he felt he had to be especially careful at all times, scanning for the next threat. The memory itself did not help: he often felt the full emotional intensity of that night—the terror, the helplessness—without any clear image to attach it to. The experience felt alien, like it belonged to someone else, and he could not put the moments in the right order. This confusion only deepened his sense that there was something broken inside him.

The cycle tightened over the years. Each time a trigger produced a startle or a wave of hypervigilance, he would try to suppress the thought, but suppression seemed to make the emotional flashbacks more fragmented and intrusive. The more he avoided media and positive feelings, the more sensitive his stress system became, so that even a routine hospital smell could send him back into that disembodied fear. He also began to engage in small, risky behaviors—driving faster than he should, leaving the house without his phone—as if courting danger to prove he could handle it, though this only heightened his constant vigilance. The threat state itself interfered with his ability to sequence the trauma memory, leaving him with only the raw affect.

Now, at 77, the strain has taken a relational toll. He has stopped visiting his grandchildren because the noise of their play—unexpected loud sounds—triggers a startle he cannot explain to them. His wife reports that he sits in silence for hours, staring at nothing. What finally brought him to seek help was a morning in the kitchen when the smell of burnt toast sent him to the floor, sobbing, without a clear image of why. He is terrified that his mind is failing, but he also hopes, quietly, that someone can help him make sense of the disarray.
